text:
Products › Conversational AI Avatar Interview

## The same interview,
the fortieth time.

A composed assessor that never drifts from the script

An avatar conducts the round, and it asks the fortieth candidate exactly what it asked the first. No fatigue, no rapport bias, no half-remembered follow-up — the script is the script, and every answer meets the same rubric.

Book a demo
See the script controls

Runs in the browser. Nothing for the candidate to install.

The same eight questions, asked identically, forty times over.

## Your best interviewer is worse
at four in the afternoon.

Interviewer variance is the largest uncontrolled variable in most hiring processes, and nobody measures it. An avatar removes it by construction: the questions, the order, the wording and the manner are identical for candidate one and candidate forty.

- No fatigue drift. The fortieth round of the week is delivered exactly like the first — same questions, same order, same wording, same pacing.
- No rapport bias. A candidate who happens to remind the interviewer of themselves gets no head start, because there is nobody there to warm to.
- Identical manner for everyone. A composed, even presentation, so a nervous candidate is not reading tension in the interviewer’s face and adjusting to it.
- Adaptive, but bounded. A thin answer draws a follow-up — and the follow-up comes from your question set rather than being improvised on the spot.
- The same rubric as the other two rounds. An avatar score, a recorded score and a live score are directly comparable, so the modality is a logistics choice rather than a scoring one.

## Round in progress — script fidelity

## One script. Every candidate.

Five stages, and the middle three are identical for everybody. That is the entire point.

## What the Avatar round does

What “runs the same script” actually means+
Not just the same list of questions. The same wording, the same order, the same pacing, and the same manner of asking — because a question delivered warmly and a question delivered flatly are not the same question. A structured interview only produces comparable results if the delivery is comparable too, and that is the part a human interviewer cannot hold constant across forty rounds in a week.
Bounded follow-ups+
A thin answer still gets probed — but the probe is selected from your own question set rather than invented in the moment. That keeps the round adaptive without reintroducing the variance the avatar exists to remove. You can see exactly which follow-ups are available for each question before a single candidate takes it.
The check before the round, and the disclosure+
The candidate runs a short check on camera, microphone and connection, and identity and document collection is handled in chat first. They are also told, before the round begins, that the interviewer is an avatar. Nobody should discover that halfway through a job interview.
Scoring, and the evidence underneath it+
Every answer is scored against your rubric by a model tier reserved for scoring, validated against a fixed schema rather than accepted as free text. Each score links back to the transcript excerpt and the moment of video it came from, so a rating can be traced to something the candidate actually said.
Body language and sentiment+
Posture, eye contact, gestures and composure are turned into structured, reviewable signal. Worth noting that an avatar round changes the baseline here — candidates behave differently when there is no human face watching — so treat it as one input among several rather than a verdict.
Pipelines, leaderboards and evaluation+
Candidates move through pipelines with weighted scorecards and leaderboards. Hiring managers rate the same recorded round rather than a summary of it, and transcripts and analytics are retained for reporting on the process itself.

## Consistency is the claim.
So is the disclosure.

An avatar interview is a stronger claim than a recorded one, so it carries a heavier obligation.

## A human makes the call

It ranks and evidences. It does not reject anyone. The hire, the pass and the pipeline stage are decisions a named person takes, on the record.

## One AI gateway, no loose ends

Every model call passes through a single choke point with schema validation, caching, per-tenant rate limits and spend caps. There is no second path to a provider.

## Media behind signed links

Recordings sit in private storage reached only through short-lived signed URLs, with lifecycle rules that expire media on a schedule.

And plainly. An avatar is not a person, candidates are told so before they start, and some of them will not want to be interviewed this way — which is a legitimate preference and a reason to offer the 2-Way round as well. Consistency is not the same as fairness: an identical script applied to everybody is a genuine improvement on interviewer variance, but a badly written script is now badly written for all forty candidates instead of some of them. We publish no accuracy figure for the scoring. And an avatar round is a screening instrument — it is not a substitute for meeting somebody before you hire them.

## Frequently asked questions

Does the candidate need to install anything to take the interview?+
No. The interview runs in the browser, so there is nothing for the candidate to install.

Are candidates told they are being interviewed by an AI avatar, and what happens before the round starts?+
Yes, candidates are told before the round begins that the interviewer is an avatar. Before that, they run a short check on camera, microphone and connection, and identity and document collection is handled in chat first.

How are answers scored, and can I see why a candidate got a particular score?+
Every answer is scored against your rubric by a model tier reserved for scoring, and the output is validated against a fixed schema rather than accepted as free text. Each score links back to the transcript excerpt and the moment of video it came from, so you can trace a rating to what the candidate actually said.

Can the avatar ask follow-up questions, or does it only read a fixed list?+
It probes thin answers with follow-ups, but each probe is selected from your own question set rather than invented in the moment, so the round stays adaptive without reintroducing interviewer variance. You can see exactly which follow-ups are available for each question before any candidate takes it.

Can I compare avatar interview scores with scores from a recorded video interview or a live two-way interview?+
Yes. All three rounds use the same rubric, so an avatar score, a recorded score and a live score are directly comparable, and choosing the format becomes a logistics decision rather than a scoring one.

Can an avatar interview replace meeting candidates in person?+
No. The avatar round is a screening instrument, not a substitute for meeting somebody before you hire them, and TalbotIQ publishes no accuracy figure for the scoring.

text:
Products › Business Management System

## Order to cash.
Purchase to pay.

An ERP built around how an SME actually runs

Five lanes, one chain of records. A quotation becomes an order, an order becomes a delivery, a delivery becomes an invoice — and the money questions read off that same chain rather than a spreadsheet kept beside it.

Book a walkthrough
Follow a sale through

Stock on hand, unit cost and ageing are derived from movements — never typed.

5

lanes, one chain

47

named steps, each on a screen

1

ledger behind every report

0

figures typed twice

One quotation, followed all the way to a collected payment.

## Selling —
order to cash

Every document carries the last one’s lines. Nothing is retyped between a quotation and an invoice, and nothing is advertised as agreed until the customer’s own paperwork says so.

Quotation
v1, v2, v3. Composed whole on one page.

Customer PO
Their number on the order, enforced where required.

Sales order
Carries the quotation’s lines.

Delivery order
Picked against what is owed and what is on the shelf.

Invoice
Amount, collected, outstanding — and every receipt against it.

Collected
Allocated against invoices; the rest says it is unallocated.

-
A revision is a new version, not an edit. v2 carries every line and supersedes v1 the moment it is issued. v1 is never edited, so what the customer actually saw is still on the record.

-
A discount past a seller’s limit becomes a draft. Not a warning they can dismiss — the line saves as a draft for somebody whose limit actually covers it.

-
“Awaiting customer PO” is a view, not a status. Accepted with no order yet, and how long it has been waiting. A customer marked requires-PO cannot have an order confirmed without one, and the composer says so.

-
A delivery can come back. Every movement is reversed and the order owes it again — because a returned delivery is a stock event, not a note in a comment field.

-
Five standing reminders per invoice, derived from the terms and each recorded once by a database constraint rather than by a job that might run twice. Raising a dispute quiets them.

-
Every ending is a recorded one. Lost with a reason, closed short with a reason, disputed with grounds, written off to bad debt with a reason and posted, or credited line by line.

Cost and margin are withheld by the server, not hidden by the interface — a money-blind role cannot see them even if it asks. A seller sees their own customers; the owner sees everyone.

## Buying —
purchase to pay

A bill cannot be paid until it agrees with the order and the goods. The three documents are checked against each other, which is the whole point of running procurement in one place.

Purchase request
By department, against a cost centre. No prices.

Approval
Nowhere until someone with the right puts their name to it.

RFQ & award
Line by line, a supplier each. The recommendation states its basis.

Purchase order
Preview, approve, then send. Approving is not sending.

GRN
Count what came. A difference needs a reason.

Bill & payment
Checked against the PO and the GRN before it can be paid.

-
The store never sees a price. A purchase request picks items by category with no prices on it at all, so whoever is asking is not anchored by what it costs.

-
The recommendation is overridable, and states its basis. Comparison runs line by line with a supplier each, so a split award is normal rather than a workaround.

-
Approving a purchase order is not sending it. Preview, then approve if you are authorised, then send or download — three separate acts, because signing off and issuing are different decisions.

-
Awaiting delivery is a standing item every day until something arrives — not a report someone remembers to open.

-
A payment run posts both sides. Debit accounts payable, credit bank — AP and the bank move together, so the two can never disagree about the same payment.

Department personnel see their own vendors; the department owner sees all of them. Scope is a property of the record rather than a filter someone chooses.

## Three more
lanes

Not everything a business pays for arrives on a pallet, and not every question is answered by a document.

Expenses & payments — no stock, so no GRN+

Raised by a department, approved, then paid like any other liability — but the kind of thing it is matters. An expense hits the P&L and the cash flow; a payment — a loan, hire purchase, SST, EPF — hits the cash flow only. And the kind is enforced: a request whose own words say loan or EPF cannot claim to be an expense.

Recurring, fixed: cost centre, vendor, due date, frequency, amount. The agreement, a start and an end are required — a fixed template without them fails the import rather than sitting there half-defined.

Recurring, variable: a budgeted amount stands in until the real bill arrives, and the instance reads No bill yet, in red, until it does. Overdue means billed and unpaid. The two are different failures and the schedule says which one you have.

The schedule runs from three months back to each agreement’s end, with status derived per row — and what is not yet due is blank, not zero, because zero is an answer and blank is the absence of one.

Inventory — by store, and no ringgit in the lane+

A trading firm has one store or two. A factory has three — raw, production, finished — each a store in its own right with its own count and its own adjustments.

Stock on hand is calculated per store from movements. It is never typed. Stock in comes from a supplier; stock out goes to a customer. A stock take is per store and the variance is journaled with a reason. An adjustment is reason-coded and journaled too.

Units are handled properly: bought by the carton, sold by the piece, with the selling cost derived from the vendor’s cost divided by the units in the carton rather than entered by hand.

And the whole lane is money-blind. No ringgit figure reaches it — the warehouse works in quantities, which is both simpler for them and safer for you.

Finance — where the money questions live+

AR ageing answers who owes you and for how long. AP ageing answers who you owe and by when. Collections is a Finance workspace for the chasing, the promises and the outcomes. Payments covers what went out, and the unallocated ones that came in.

A customer statement of account is the customer’s copy of the same ledger — not a separately maintained document that can drift from it.

e-Invoice: MyInvois validation state travels on the invoice itself rather than living in a separate submission log.

A 13-week cash runway is computed from what is expected in and expected out. See the build state below for what in this lane is designed rather than finished.

Why it is one chain and not five modules+

Every step in the process names the screen it happens on, and the application refuses to start if a step names a screen that does not exist. That sounds like an implementation detail; it is actually the reason the flow above is accurate. A process map that is generated from the code cannot describe a workflow the software does not have.

The same discipline runs through the data. Stock on hand is derived from movements. Unit cost is derived from the purchase cost and the pack size. Ageing is derived from the invoice and its terms. Reminders are derived from the invoice date. None of them is a field somebody maintains, which is why the reports cannot disagree with the documents.

## Where this actually is

Forty-seven steps, each with a build state we track rather than round up. Here it is, honestly, so a conversation starts from the right place.

15

Live
Working and walked end to end by an automated suite, not demoed by hand.

25

Partly built
The step works; something named is still outstanding. Each one says what.

7

Designed, not built
Specified and scheduled, with no screen yet. Named below rather than implied.

The seven not yet built: the cash flow statement, the income and expense statement, both budgets, bank statement import, bank reconciliation, and production value-add for factories. The SST statement is deliberately held until the treatment is verified with RMCD — we would rather ship it late than ship it wrong.

Also still to come across the partly-built steps: document uploads on the six steps that want one, part payments and multi-invoice settlement, store-to-store transfers, and e-Invoice submission with a register of what is pending. There is no customer portal — a quotation is sent as a PDF, and a login for customers waits until one asks for it.

Nothing in the five lanes above describes a step that does not exist. What is unfinished is on this list.

## Derived, not
maintained.

Three properties that decide whether an ERP is trusted a year in or quietly worked around.

## Every figure is computed

Stock on hand, unit cost, ageing and reminder dates are all derived from the records underneath them. No second set of numbers exists to fall out of step.

## Scope is enforced on the server

A money-blind role cannot retrieve cost or margin, whatever the interface asks for. Sellers see their own customers, departments see their own vendors.

## Every ending has a reason on it

Lost, closed short, disputed, written off, credited, adjusted, counted short — each one records why, so the exceptions are as auditable as the happy path.

Sales CRM
Deals and quotations for a sales team, where the ERP takes over at the order.

ATS
Recruitment end to end — in Agency Mode, a placement is the invoice the ERP raises.

How does the inventory module handle stock across more than one store or warehouse?+

## Blind assessment. And it knows
when a model wrote it.

Behavioural text interviews, assessed blind

Behavioural questions answered in text, assessed with no name, no face and no accent attached — and with AI-generated answers detected as they arrive rather than discovered three rounds later.

Book a demo
See how detection works

Any device, any connection. Nothing to install and nothing to schedule.

MCQsA declared answer set, so the score is arithmetic. Timed Q&AA visible clock per question. Recall, not research. Conversational Chat InterviewOpen-ended, with follow-ups that go deeper.

Closed answers, constrained answers, open answers — three instruments with one rubric behind them, so a knowledge score and a conversation score sit on the same axis.

## Everyone has the same model open
in the next tab.

A written screening question stopped being a signal the moment a language model could answer it perfectly. So this round detects that as the answer arrives, and keeps the two things a text round is uniquely good at: blindness, and thinking time.

- AI-generated answers are flagged in real time — while the round is running, not after somebody notices three candidates wrote the same suspiciously polished paragraph.
- Blind by construction. No name, no photograph, no accent, no appearance, no age cue. Just the answer against the rubric, which is the strongest structural bias control of the three rounds.
- Written communication as the actual skill. For support, documentation, legal, marketing and any remote-first role, how somebody writes under a prompt is the job rather than a proxy for it.
- Thinking time is a feature, not a loophole. A candidate who freezes on camera and writes clearly is a candidate you would otherwise never have seen.
- Knowledge checks in the same round. Multiple-choice items drawn from your own question sets sit alongside the behavioural questions, so a factual screen does not need a second tool.

## Round in progress — support engineer

QDescribe a time you gave a customer an answer they would not like.

A“A merchant’s payouts were held by our risk system. I couldn’t release them, so I told them that plainly and got them a written timeline the same afternoon…”Scored

QHow do you decide what to escalate?

A“Escalation should be guided by a holistic assessment of impact, urgency and stakeholder alignment…”
no specifics · register shift from the previous answerFlagged

Blind: no name, no photo, no accent on this screen · a flag goes to the reviewer, never to a rejection

## No scheduling. No camera. No excuses.

Five stages, and the lightest round of the three. Identity is settled first, so everything after it is about the answers.

Invite sent

automatic

Identity first

in chat

real time

## What the Chat Interview does

Blind by construction, not by policy+
The reviewer sees the answers against the rubric. No name, no photograph, no accent, no appearance, no age cue — because none of them are on the screen to begin with. That is a structural bias control rather than a training reminder, and it is the reason a text round is worth running even when you could run a video one.
Detecting an answer a model wrote+
AI-generated answers are detected in real time, while the round is running. The flag goes to the reviewer with its reasoning attached — and it is a flag, not a rejection. Nobody is removed from a pipeline by a detector; a person looks and decides. That distinction matters, because a false positive here costs somebody a job.
Identity and documents, collected first+
Before the questions begin, identity and document collection is handled in the chat itself. Everything after that is about the answers, and you are never reviewing somebody whose paperwork turns out to be missing at the offer stage.
Question sets, adaptive follow-ups and knowledge checks+
Reusable question sets grouped into sections, with multiple-choice items mixed in where a factual screen is what you need. The interview adapts as it goes, so a thin answer draws a follow-up. Question generation runs in the background, so a new role does not wait on somebody writing a bank from scratch.
Scoring, with the excerpt attached+
Every answer is scored against your rubric by a model tier reserved for scoring, validated against a fixed schema rather than accepted as free text. Each score links to the answer it came from — and because this is the same rubric the video and voice rounds use, a chat score and a live-round score sit on one axis.
Pipelines, leaderboards and evaluation+
Candidates move through pipelines with weighted scorecards and leaderboards, so evaluation lives in one place instead of five inboxes. Hiring managers assess the same answers rather than a summary of them, and transcripts and analytics are retained for reporting on the process itself.

## A flag is not
a verdict

Detection is the most consequential thing on this page, so it is the one with the most restraint built around it.

## A human makes the call

It ranks, evidences and flags. It does not reject anyone. A flagged answer is surfaced with its reason for a person to judge, never auto-removed from a pipeline.

## One AI gateway, no loose ends

Every model call passes through a single choke point with schema validation, caching, per-tenant rate limits and spend caps. There is no second path to a provider.

## Blind is the default state

Identifying detail is absent from the assessment screen rather than hidden behind a toggle somebody can switch off on a busy afternoon.

And plainly, about detection. No detector is perfect, and we publish no accuracy figure for this one — a percentage from somebody else’s dataset tells you nothing about your applicants. That is exactly why a flag is shown with its reasoning and never acts on its own: the cost of a false positive is a person losing a job they were qualified for. Treat it as a prompt to read the answer properly, not as a result. A text round also cannot assess spoken fluency or presence — that is what the Voice and Video rounds are for.

Voice InterviewWhen speaking is the skill — the same rubric, spoken and transcribed.Video InterviewWhen you need the round back, and the non-verbal signal with it.

## Frequently asked questions

Does the candidate need to install an app or book a time slot to take the interview?+
No. It runs on any device over any connection, with nothing to install and nothing to schedule. There is no camera either.

If the interview is blind, how is the candidate's identity verified?+
Identity and document collection is handled in the chat itself before the questions begin. Everything after that is about the answers, so you are not reviewing someone whose paperwork turns out to be missing at the offer stage.

Will the AI-writing detector automatically reject a candidate, and how accurate is it?+
No. A flag is shown to the reviewer with its reasoning attached and never acts on its own; a person reads the answer and decides. TalbotIQ states that no detector is perfect and publishes no accuracy figure for this one, on the basis that a percentage from someone else's dataset says nothing about your applicants and a false positive can cost a qualified person a job.

How are the written answers scored?+
Every answer is scored against your rubric by a model tier reserved for scoring, and the output is validated against a fixed schema rather than accepted as free text. Each score links back to the answer it came from, and the rubric is the same one used by the video and voice rounds, so a chat score and a live-round score sit on one axis.

Can I add multiple-choice knowledge questions to the same text interview?+
Yes. Reusable question sets are grouped into sections, with multiple-choice items from your own question sets mixed in where you need a factual screen, so it does not need a second tool. The interview also adapts as it goes, so a thin answer draws a follow-up question.

When is a text interview the wrong choice?+
When you need to assess spoken fluency or presence, which a text round cannot do. That is what the Voice and Video rounds are for: the Voice Interview uses the same rubric, spoken and transcribed, and the Video Interview is for when you need the round itself back, along with the non-verbal signal.

structured data.

Contact and receipt intelligence

AI extraction reads business cards and receipts in any language, pulls out every field, converts currencies and flags tampering — with local OCR as an automatic offline fallback, and a person confirming before anything is saved.

Book a demo

## It tells you what it
is not sure about.

Extraction is the easy half. The hard half is knowing which of the twelve fields it just filled in you should actually check — so the Intelligent Document Management marks them, next to the original photograph, before you commit anything.

- Per-field confidence, not one score for the document. Fields below the threshold are highlighted individually, so you verify the two that are doubtful rather than re-reading all twelve.
- The photo sits beside the form. You check the flagged value against the paper without hunting for the original.
- Warnings arrive before the confirm, not after. A receipt carries a tamper-risk flag, a blurry-image flag and a duplicate check — because a receipt becomes money against a cost centre, and "this image may have been altered" is not something to learn later.
- It refuses to invent a person. A card whose name could not actually be read is rejected rather than saved with a placeholder in the name field — added after one came back reading IMAGE NOT INCLUDED at high confidence and the review pane presented it as somebody's name.
- What you correct is what gets saved. Your edits win, and the original extraction is kept underneath rather than overwritten.

## What the Intelligent Document Management does

Two document types, done properly+
Business cards and receipts. Nothing else — not invoices, purchase orders, contracts or identity documents. From a card you get the full name, company, job title, department, the primary email and every other email found, the primary phone and every other phone, the address broken into city, state, postal code and country, a LinkedIn URL and notes. From a receipt: merchant name and address, receipt number, transaction date, currency, total, tax, discount, payment method, expense category and the individual line items.
Any language, any currency+
The reader is not tuned to one script or one locale. It reads the document in whatever language it was printed in and translates as it extracts, so a receipt in Malay, Mandarin or Tamil comes back as the same structured fields as an English one. Amounts are converted and the base currency is recorded alongside the original, so a figure is never ambiguous about which currency it is in.
Recovering from a bad scan without retaking it+
Read again re-extracts the image you already uploaded, so a poor first pass does not mean finding the card again. Merge folds a duplicate into the original — gaps filled, emails and phone numbers combined rather than one overwriting the other. Link later attaches a capture to a record after the fact. And a manual receipt lets you type one that never had a photograph, so a cash fare sits beside the scanned costs instead of in a separate note.
It works when the connection does not+
Extraction runs on AI vision where it can and falls back to local optical character recognition automatically when it cannot — so capture in a basement car park or on a plane still produces something to review later, rather than an error and a lost receipt.
The original extraction is never thrown away+
Every capture keeps what the model originally read alongside what you confirmed, with the edit history attached. That matters twice: you can see what was changed and by whom, and it is the honest basis for measuring how often review actually corrects something — which is a real number about this product rather than a claimed accuracy figure.
Taking the data out+
Cards export to CSV, Excel, JSON and vCard, so a stack of business cards becomes contacts your phone can import directly. Receipts export to CSV, Excel, JSON and PDF. There is no lock-in step and nothing needs an integration to be useful — the export is the integration.

## Extraction is automatic.
The write is not.

A document intelligence tool that saves silently is a data-entry tool with extra steps. Three things make the difference.

## A person confirms every record

A capture moves through processing, then waits in review. It becomes a contact or a cost only when somebody has read it and said yes — and it can be discarded instead. There is no automatic write path.

## Your library is only yours

Every query is scoped to the signed-in account. Nothing in the product exposes one person's captures to another, and a scanned business card is by definition somebody else's personal data being held on your behalf.

## Warnings before the decision

Tamper risk, blur, duplicates, missing fields and per-field confidence are all surfaced at the moment you are deciding — not recorded quietly for an audit nobody runs.

And what it does not do. One account, one library. There are no teams, no sharing and no delegation anywhere in the product — you cannot give your accountant access, and a bookkeeper cannot hold a client's library on their behalf. Two document types only, images only. Capture by emailing or messaging a document in is built but not switched on, so today it is upload and camera. Reconciling receipts against a bank statement is in the product, but the suggestion queue is not yet available. And we publish no accuracy figure, because nothing in the product measures accuracy against a ground truth — what we can show you instead is how often a human corrected a field, which is a real number from your own library rather than a claim about ours.

TalbotIQ makes nine interview formats, the recruitment software that turns a scorecard into a pipeline stage, and six business tools: a sales CRM, a business management system (ERP) for SMEs, a task and productivity manager, document management, a meeting note taker, and the private AI engine every product runs on.

The interview formats run on Mimic, the interview platform: you define one rubric, candidates take their round in a browser or on the phone they already have, and the platform recommends. It never rejects anyone; a named person makes every decision.

- One rubric across the scored formats, with each score linked to the transcript or moment it came from, so a first-round score and a final-round score sit on the same axis.

## No model decides
anything here.

Every other round on this site involves a model forming a view, which is why they all carry a “a human decides” caveat. This one does not. You declare the correct options, the candidate picks, and the result is counted.

- The answer set is declared up front. Scoring is arithmetic rather than judgement — which means there is nothing to appeal, and nothing to explain to a candidate who asks how they were marked.

## What the MCQ round does

A declared answer set, and why that matters+
The correct options are recorded before a single candidate sits the round, so the result is a count rather than an assessment. That has a practical consequence worth naming: this is the only round in the suite where a candidate asking “how was I marked” gets an answer you can show them in full, without discussing rubrics, models or reasoning.
Question banks, sections and randomisation+
Reusable banks grouped into sections, so a round tests regulatory knowledge, product detail and process separately and reports each one. Questions and their options can be randomised, so two candidates sitting simultaneously are not reading the same screen in the same order — a modest control, honestly described.
Instant results and the floors you set+
Scored on submit, with no review queue. You can set a floor per section rather than only an overall pass mark, which is usually what you actually want: somebody strong overall but below the line on the regulated section is a different decision from somebody uniformly average.
Where MCQs are the right instrument — and where they are not+
They are the right instrument for a threshold: does this person know the regulated thing, the safety procedure, the product. They are a poor instrument for a ranking, because the gap between 13 and 15 out of 15 tells you very little about who will do the job better. Use it to filter, then use a written or spoken round to choose.
Mixing into a longer round+
Multiple-choice items can sit inside a conversational or timed round rather than running separately, which is often the better shape — a few factual checks in among the behavioural questions, in one sitting, without asking a candidate to complete two separate things.
Pipelines and reporting+
Results land on the candidate record and the pipeline like any other score, and because they are deterministic they are the cleanest thing in your reporting — useful for showing how a cohort performed against a knowledge requirement over time.

## It is a knowledge floor,
not a knowledge test

This round is the most honest and the most limited thing in the suite, and both facts matter equally.

## Scoring is arithmetic

The answer set is declared before the round exists. There is no model judgement, no rubric interpretation, and nothing for a candidate to appeal.

## The threshold is your decision

The software counts. What counts as a pass, per section and overall, is set by you and recorded — so a decision can be explained months later.

## Deterministic by design

Same answers, same score, every time. It is the one part of the pipeline where the result cannot drift between two runs.

And plainly, the big one. There is no proctoring. A candidate sitting an MCQ round at home can look things up, and for most questions a model will answer them correctly in seconds. So treat this as a knowledge floor — evidence somebody could find and apply the right answer — rather than proof they knew it unaided. If unaided recall is genuinely what you need to measure, that is what Timed Q&A is for, and even then a clock is a constraint rather than a guarantee. MCQs also measure recall rather than judgement, so they should filter a pipeline and never choose from one.

## What Mimic does

Candidate onboarding and system check+
Before a round starts, the candidate runs a short check on camera, microphone and connection, with identity and document collection handled in chat first. Interviewers only reach people who are validated and ready, and nobody loses a round to a broken headset.
Question management that adapts+
Reusable question sets grouped into sections, multiple choice mixed in, and an interview that adapts as it goes. Question generation runs in the background, so a new role doesn't wait on someone writing a bank from scratch.
Invitations that send themselves+
Applicants are invited automatically as they apply, handled by a background worker rather than a person remembering. That is what makes same-day interviewing possible at volume.
Scoring, results and evidence+
Every answer is scored against your rubric by a model tier reserved for scoring, validated against a fixed schema rather than accepted as free text. Each score links back to the transcript excerpt it came from, so a rating can always be traced to something the candidate actually said.
Sentiment and body-language analysis+
AI reads emotional tone and confidence — posture, eye contact, gestures, composure — turning non-verbal signals into structured, reviewable intelligence rather than an interviewer's gut feel written down afterwards.
Pipelines, analytics and centralised evaluation+
Candidates move through pipelines with weighted scorecards and leaderboards, so evaluation lives in one place. Hiring managers rate the same recorded round rather than a summary of it, and transcripts and analytics are retained for reporting.

## Candidate data is somebody's career

Recordings, transcripts and scores are the most sensitive data you will hold about a person who doesn't yet work for you.

## A human makes the call

Mimic ranks and evidences. It does not reject anyone. The hire, the pass and the pipeline stage are all decisions a person takes, on the record.

## One AI gateway, no loose ends

Every model call passes through a single choke point with schema validation, caching, per-tenant rate limits and spend caps. There is no second path to a provider.

## Media behind signed links

Recordings sit in private storage reached only through short-lived signed URLs, with lifecycle rules that expire media on a schedule rather than keeping it forever.

Does the AI decide who gets rejected, or does a person?+
A person does. Mimic interviews and scores candidates against your rubric with the evidence attached, but the decision is made by humans: the product is described as screening intelligence decided by humans, and the final stage of its five-stage process is labelled "You decide".

Yes. You pick the mode that fits the role and the stage, and scoring is identical across modes, so a chat score and a live-round score sit on the same axis and can be compared directly.

Recordings sit in private storage that is reached only through short-lived signed URLs. Lifecycle rules expire media on a schedule rather than keeping it indefinitely.

## Scheduling is the bottleneck.
Interviewing never was.

Nobody shortlists forty people because interviewing is hard. They shortlist because finding forty mutually convenient half-hours is impossible. Take the calendar out and the constraint disappears.

## What the Recorded round does

Takes and think time — what the candidate controls+
Both are yours to set, per question. One take tests composure and gives you something close to a live answer. Three takes tests thinking, and tells you what somebody produces when they can gather themselves. Think time works the same way: thirty seconds is a pressure test, two minutes is a reasoning test. Deciding this deliberately is most of what separates a useful recorded round from a bad one.
The check before the round+
Before recording anything, the candidate runs a short check on camera, microphone and connection, and identity and document collection is handled in chat first. Nobody loses a round to a broken headset, and you only review people who were validated and ready. It all happens in the browser, with nothing to install.
Question sets that adapt+
Reusable question sets grouped into sections, with multiple-choice items mixed in where a knowledge check makes sense, and an interview that adapts based on what has been answered. Question generation runs in the background, so a newly opened role does not wait on somebody writing a bank from scratch.
Scoring, with the moment attached+
Answers are scored against your rubric by a model tier reserved for scoring, validated against a fixed schema rather than accepted as free text. Each score links back to the transcript excerpt and the moment of video it came from — which is what lets a panel settle a disagreement by watching rather than arguing.
Body language and sentiment+
Posture, eye contact, gestures and composure are turned into structured, reviewable signal. It is one input among several. A candidate recording at eleven at night in a shared flat is not short of composure, and the page would be lying if it implied otherwise.
Parallel review, pipelines and leaderboards+
The real second bottleneck in hiring is getting three busy people into the same room. Here they each watch the same round whenever they can, rating against weighted scorecards, with the results collected in one pipeline rather than three inboxes.

## A recording of somebody’s
career

Video is the most sensitive thing you will hold about a person who does not yet work for you.

## A human makes the call

It ranks and evidences. It does not reject anyone. The hire, the pass and the pipeline stage are decisions a named person takes, on the record.

## One AI gateway, no loose ends

Every model call passes through a single choke point with schema validation, caching, per-tenant rate limits and spend caps. There is no second path to a provider.

## Media behind signed links

Recordings sit in private storage reached only through short-lived signed URLs, with lifecycle rules that expire media on a schedule.

A recorded round is a screening instrument, not a conversation — the candidate cannot ask you anything, and for a senior or a competitive hire that asymmetry is a real cost, which is what the 2-Way round is for. It also needs a camera, a microphone and somewhere passable to sit, so the Voice and Chat rounds exist for candidates who have none of those. We publish no accuracy figure for the scoring. For internal talent teams. Every recruitment module, plus the approval layer that keeps headcount honest before it is advertised.

The module you get

Manpower Requisitions

Headcount asked for, costed and approved before a job exists. A requisition has no applicants and no pipeline — it becomes a job only once approved, so nothing is advertised unfunded.

-
Five requisition types — new headcount, replacement, internal backfill, project-based or budgeted growth, and the type is one thing approval routes on.

-
Cost on the record — the salary band and annualised budget sit on the requisition, because that is what an approver is being asked to sign.

-
Chains name roles, not people — and every decision is stamped with who made it and when.

-
Routing you configure — rules match on level, business unit, budget or salary band, first match wins, and a test tool shows which rule claims a seat.

Agency Mode

## Filling roles for clients

For staffing firms and RPOs who fill roles for clients and bill them. Every recruitment module, plus the commercial layer that keeps the client relationship on the same record.

The module you get instead

Customer Management

One record per client, holding the paper, the people and the deals it carries. Every job for that client belongs to the account, so the rate card follows the placement.

-
Contracts as data — term dates, approver, payment terms and value are fields, with the signed PDF attached, so an agreement can be reported on.

-
Banded rate cards — the agreed fee is held as a scale in bands on the agreement rather than a single number.

-
Deals raised off a contract — Create Opportunity inherits the agreed terms, so the commercial basis of a deal is never retyped.

-
Feeds the commercial book — pipeline value, weighted pipeline, win rate and confidence bands all report from these records.

Identical in both modes

Dashboard

Jobs

Candidates

Offer letters

Resume parser

Matching

## Every record
becomes the next one.

One login and one database behind all of it. An approved requisition becomes a job, a parsed resume becomes a candidate, an applicant becomes an offer.

Requisition

Costed and approved before anything is advertised.

Job

Ten tabs, seven stages, its own apply address.

Parsed

Six named stages. Nothing auto-imported.

Candidate

Ranked against the brief, score printed on the row.

Signed offer

Nineteen field types, executed on the document.

In Agency Mode the chain starts one step earlier. A client contract becomes a deal, and the deal becomes the job — so the rate card agreed with the client follows the placement all the way to the invoice.

## What each module
gives you

Jobs — a record, not an advert+

Ten tabs on one job: overview, applications, pipeline, recommended, interviews, publishing, notes, activities, documents and email. Five saved views you work from rather than filters to rebuild every morning — assigned to me, active, all, draft, completed. Creation runs in four gated steps: job information, JD generator, templates and commercials, then overview and posting. The seven-stage pipeline is applied, screening, interview, assessment, offer, hired and rejected, and dragging a card advances the applicant and stamps the trail. Professional and soft skills each carry a weighting plus the share of applicants holding them, and matching scores against it. Every job has its own inbound email address, so an application arriving by mail lands on the record.

Candidates — a database you can actually work+

Not a folder of CVs. The row itself carries candidate, top skills, experience, score, live applications and status, so a shortlist needs no clicks. Seven tabs per person: CV, applied jobs, interviews, offers, compliance, documents and activity. The original document is kept and parsed out as data, which is what makes someone findable. One person can be live on several roles at once with the stage and score they hold on each. Compliance is tracked as individually named requirements in packs, so “not cleared” always says which item is actually outstanding. And every change, stage move and message is dated and attributed — the next recruiter inherits the context, not just the CV.

Resume parser — six stages you can watch+

Ten files a batch, with the limit stated on screen and a counter for the room left. Six named stages: uploading, extracting text, detecting sections, extracting fields, normalising and scoring, then matching candidates. A live activity log writes out every step as it happens and is retained after the run. The stages are named for a reason — a file that fails points at the stage it failed on rather than reporting an error. Full name and email are required; phone, location and summary are not, so a partial parse is still usable. And nothing is auto-imported: results are reviewed first, and creating the candidate is a separate, deliberate action.

Candidate matching — the database ranks itself+

Selecting a job loads its own skills, experience band and location as the starting criteria, so a search begins from the brief. Five criteria — skills, job title, experience, education, location — each switching on independently and contributing nothing until it does, with a slider deciding how hard each one pulls. The score is printed on every row, so a low match can be judged on its merits rather than quietly hidden. The whole database is ranked, not a top five cut off at an arbitrary line, which is what makes the long tail usable. Rows are selectable for bulk action, and a criteria set can be saved and run again.

Offer letters — not a mail merge+

A searchable template library — standard offer, contract engagement, internship, executive — each carrying its own fields, with the candidate’s personal information, address, preferences and compensation sitting beside the document so a letter is filled, not retyped. Nineteen placeable field types in four groups: the ones that execute the letter (signature, initial, stamp, data sign), text elements (text, number, checkbox, radio, dropdown, date, table), personal data pulled from the record, and extend elements including image, attachment, approve and decline. Approve, decline and reset live on the letter itself, and the outcome lands on the candidate’s offer tab and the job’s pipeline.

Dashboard and settings — configuration, not code+

Four live counters against last month, the pipeline funnel with headcount and conversion at each of the seven stages, recent jobs, AI match alerts since you last looked, and a dated activity feed drawn from every module. Job status mix, source attribution and recruiter KPIs against target sit on the same page — analytics without a BI seat. Underneath, settings covers users and five roles with each role’s permissions listed rather than implied, job code format and pipeline stages, candidate settings including duplicate detection, consent and retention periods, KPI targets with monthly bands, and the template libraries and named approval routes reused by every record.

without a person saying so.

Three properties that make an AI-assisted pipeline defensible when a candidate, an auditor or a hiring manager asks why.

## Nothing auto-imported

The parser produces results; it does not create records. A parsed CV is reviewed, and creating the candidate is a separate, deliberate action.

## Explainable ranking

The score is printed on every row and the criteria are visible and weighted, so a low match is judged on its merits rather than quietly filtered out of view.

## Derived, never entered

Every dashboard figure is computed from the live record, so the reporting cannot drift from the pipeline it describes. Nobody maintains a second set of numbers.

And plainly. The AI ranks, parses and drafts — it does not reject anyone, and it does not create a record. Advancing a candidate, approving a requisition and signing an offer are all actions a named person takes, stamped with who and when. Matching scores the database you have; it does not source candidates you do not. And the two modes are one product on one tenant, so an agency that later hires internally does not migrate — Customer Management is switched on beside what is already there.

Mimic
AI interviews for every candidate — scorecards and leaderboards that sync back to the ATS pipeline.

ERP
The autonomous backbone — where a placement becomes an invoice and a hire becomes a person on payroll.

## Your CRM should do the typing.

A sales CRM for the desk and the road

Business cards, receipts and meetings go in as photos and audio — and a person confirms every one before it touches a record. Configurable pipeline, quote-to-cash with approval routing, and per-customer receivables.

Book a demo
See how capture works

Nothing reaches a contact or a deal without a person confirming it.

Card to contact, meeting to recap, quote to paid invoice.

## One button. Three ways in.

The same control on every screen of both apps. It reads the record you already have open, so whatever you capture attaches itself to the right deal without you choosing from a list.

Attaches to Cold-chain upgrade

Scan a documentBusiness card or receipt

Take minutesRecord the room, the tab or the call

Ask NoahQuestion your pipeline in plain language

- Two document types, done properly. Business cards and receipts. Not invoices, contracts or ID documents.

- A recording survives navigation — and the local file is deleted once uploaded.

- Noah cannot change anything. All twelve of its tools are reads, each permission-gated, and every answer names the records it read.

## Review pane — nothing saves until you confirm

CompanySeri Logistik Sdn Bhd

Job titleHead of ProcurementVerify

Phone+60 3–7?9 4412Verify

Tamper riskReceipt total may have been alteredCheck

Doubtful fields flagged beside the original photo · what you correct is what gets saved · a card with no readable name is refused

## First contact to paid invoice.

Nothing gets re-keyed along the way. Each document converts into the next, with an approval at every step and a trail back to what was agreed.

Deal on the board

routed

## And the rest of the CRM

Configurable pipeline and the deal record+
Your stages, in your order — create, rename, reorder, and mark each as a step, a win or a loss. Drag deals across the board in the browser and on the phone. Every transition is written to history, so a deal's path is reconstructable. The deal itself carries priority, category, referral source, files, line items, notes, activities on a calendar, more than one rep, and tabs for quotations, orders, invoices and meetings.
Quotations, approvals and the document chain+
Line items with per-item taxes and charges from a configured catalogue rather than one flat percentage, terms templates editable per document, and revisions that keep their history. A configurable approval matrix routes each document to the right approver by condition, with a live count of what's waiting in the top bar. Quote converts to order, order to invoice, with an approval at each step.
Payments, progress billing and receivables+
Record partial payments with proof of payment attached, and the invoice recomputes its status. Invoice a large job in slices against the agreed value, with each preview showing how many slices are live. AR ageing runs per customer across current, 1–30, 31–60, 61–90 and 91+ buckets, drillable to the invoice, plus a customer statement of account.
Noah, and seven AI actions that show their reasoning+
A deal score out of 100 with the model's own reasoning and a confidence rating. A stalled-deal check with its reason. Sentiment and risks across the notes actually logged, action items pulled from those same notes, meeting prep, category suggestion, and paste-to-fill for a contact that never auto-submits. The facts come from the database, not from the form on your screen.
Multiple companies, roles and the audit trail+
Workspaces are separate books you switch between without switching accounts. Subsidiaries sit inside one workspace, each with its own currency and tax registration. Four role presets — Owner, Sales Manager, Sales Rep, Viewer — then tune per person. Every row records who created it, and editing an already-approved document demands a typed reason that is stored against it.
The mobile app, and what it isn't+
Not a viewer — five tabs with full create and edit for contacts, customers, deals, quotes and invoices, plus scanning and recording. Tokens live in the OS keystore, sessions refresh silently, and a network blip won't sign you out. It needs a connection though: there is no offline mode, and the app is distributed directly rather than through the app stores.

## It shows its work,
including where it stops.

A CRM that shows its reasoning should be straight about its limits too.

## A person confirms everything

Extraction is automatic; the write is not. A card, a receipt or a recap only becomes a record once somebody has looked at it and said yes.

## Entity separation is enforced

Separation between subsidiaries is applied by the server rather than left to a query filter — verified in the live configuration, not just intended.

## Noah cannot write

Twelve read-only tools, each permission-gated to what you can already see, and every answer names the records it consulted.

And plainly, what it doesn't do. No offline mode. No two-factor or single sign-on. Contacts import from CSV or Excel, but there is no importer for customers, deals, quotes or history. Only cards and receipts scan. Sales orders can't be emailed, and payments are recorded rather than taken. We hold no SOC 2 or ISO 27001 certification and won't imply one. If any of that matters, it's better raised before you buy than after.

Intelligent Document Management — Document IntelligenceThe engine behind card and receipt scanning. Any language, currency conversion, tamper flags.
Intelligent Note Taker — Meeting IntelligenceThe engine behind Minute Taker. Live transcript and instant recap across Meet, Zoom and Teams.

## Frequently asked questions

Does a scanned business card or receipt go straight into the CRM, or does someone check it first?+
Someone checks it first: nothing saves until you confirm it in the review pane. Doubtful fields are flagged beside the original photo, what you correct is what gets saved, and a card with no readable name is refused.

Can the AI assistant in the CRM edit or delete my deals and contacts?+
No. Noah cannot write to anything: all twelve of its tools are read-only, each permission-gated to what you can already see, and every answer names the records it consulted.

Can the CRM produce quotations and invoices, or do I still need separate quoting software?+
It handles the chain itself: a quote converts to an order and the order to an invoice, with an approval at each step. A configurable approval matrix routes each document to the right approver by condition, with a live count of what is waiting shown in the top bar.

Can the CRM track unpaid invoices and receivables per customer?+
Yes. You record partial payments with proof of payment attached and the invoice recomputes its status, and a large job can be invoiced in slices against the agreed value. AR ageing runs per customer across current, 1–30, 31–60, 61–90 and 91+ day buckets.

Does the mobile CRM app work offline, and is it in the app stores?+
No on both counts. The mobile app needs a connection — there is no offline mode — and it is distributed directly rather than through the app stores.

What can't this CRM do that I should know before buying?+
There is no offline mode and no two-factor authentication or single sign-on. Contacts import from CSV or Excel, but there is no importer for customers, deals, quotes or history; only business cards and receipts scan; sales orders cannot be emailed; and payments are recorded rather than taken.

## A clock changes
what you are measuring.

Written answers against a visible per-question timer

Set a limit per question and you stop measuring what somebody can research. You start measuring what they actually know, how they structure it under pressure, and how they write when there is no time to polish it.

Book a demo
See the timing controls

Per-question limits you set. The clock is visible to the candidate.

Limits set per question, a round run against the clock, scored on submit.

## Sixty seconds and five minutes
are different questions.

The limit is the instrument, so it should be chosen rather than defaulted. A minute asks what somebody has at their fingertips. Five asks how they organise a thought. The same question with two different clocks tests two different things.

- Per question, not per round. A factual question gets sixty seconds; a design question gets five minutes. One limit across a whole round is almost always the wrong limit for most of it.
- The candidate can see the clock. Pressure somebody knows about is a fair test. Pressure they discover at the end is a trick, and it measures surprise rather than competence.
- It auto-submits at zero, and a partial answer is still assessed — because how far somebody got in the time is itself the signal.
- It narrows the window on model-written answers. Not closes it — narrows it. Detection runs alongside, and the two together are more useful than either alone.
- Blind assessment still applies. No name, no photograph, no accent on the review screen.
- The same rubric as MCQ and conversational rounds, so a timed score sits on the same axis as an untimed one.

## What the Timed round does

What the limit is actually testing+
Worth being precise, because this is the whole design decision. A short limit measures what is already known and how somebody performs when rushed. A long limit measures structure, completeness and judgement. Neither is better; they are different instruments. The common mistake is picking one number for the whole round and then wondering why the results are muddy.
A clock the candidate can see+
The countdown is on screen throughout. That is a deliberate fairness choice: a candidate who knows they have ninety seconds writes for ninety seconds, and one who does not know writes for as long as feels right and then loses the answer. Hidden timers measure surprise.
Timing, and answers a model wrote+
A tight limit is the most practical constraint available against pasted model output, and detection runs alongside it. Both are partial. Together they are meaningfully better than either alone, and the page would be overselling if it said more than that.
Scoring, with the excerpt attached+
Answers are scored against your rubric by a model tier reserved for scoring, validated against a fixed schema rather than accepted as free text. Each score links to the answer it came from. A partial answer that auto-submitted is scored on what is there, and the reviewer can see it ran out of time.
Question sets and adaptive follow-ups+
Reusable question sets grouped into sections, with follow-ups drawn from your own set when an answer is thin. Multiple-choice items can be mixed in with their own tighter limits. Question generation runs in the background, so a new role does not wait on somebody writing a bank.
Pipelines and evaluation+
Candidates move through pipelines with weighted scorecards and leaderboards. Per-question timings are retained alongside the answers, which is often the more interesting data — somebody who answered well in a third of the limit is telling you something.

## A clock is a constraint.
Not a guarantee.

A timed round is a stronger instrument than an untimed one and a heavier obligation. Both things are true.

## A human makes the call

It ranks, evidences and flags. It does not reject anyone. The pass, the fail and the pipeline stage are decisions a named person takes.

## One AI gateway, no loose ends

Every model call passes through a single choke point with schema validation, caching, per-tenant rate limits and spend caps. There is no second path to a provider.

## Blind is the default state

Identifying detail is absent from the assessment screen rather than hidden behind a toggle somebody can switch off on a busy afternoon.

And plainly, the part that needs saying. A timer disadvantages some people for reasons unrelated to competence — candidates writing in a second language, candidates with dyslexia or a processing difference, candidates on a slow connection or a phone keyboard. Adjusting or waiving limits where somebody needs it is your obligation, and in many jurisdictions a legal one; the software will let you set different limits, but it cannot decide when you should. A clock is also not proctoring: it narrows the window for looking something up without closing it. And we publish no accuracy figure for the scoring or the detection.

The rubric, while you are still talking+

Products › Vawlt

## Private by architecture,
not by policy.

Purpose-trained AI, served on hardware we control

27 of 33 AI tasks are answered by models that never leave our own servers — each one separately trained for its single job. The six that go outside were measured as beyond what our own models do faithfully, and the catalogue says exactly which.

Book a demo
See how routing works

Every task declares where it runs and what it does with personal data.

A task picked from the catalogue, run end to end, with the model and latency shown.

## Ask for a job.
Never for a model.

You send a task name and raw input. The engine picks the model, applies that task's privacy policy, calls it, validates the answer where the legal values are known, logs the cost against you, and returns one standard envelope. You never choose or configure a model.

- A fixed catalogue, not a general model. 35 tasks defined, 33 served, 2 withheld. An unknown task name is a hard error rather than a best guess.
- One model in memory, not thirty. A task-specific adapter is selected per request against a single resident model, so 27 specialised tasks cost roughly the memory of one.
- Keep your existing client code. An OpenAI-compatible contract runs the same pipeline — change the base URL, the key, and put a task name in the model field. Standard sampling parameters are accepted and ignored rather than rejected.
- The same input gives the same answer. Local calls run deterministically with the inference cache off. That was found the hard way: with caching on, 4 of 10 sampled tasks changed their output depending on what came before.
- The catalogue cannot go stale. Everything that answers "what tasks exist" — the manual, the live endpoint, the console picker, even the examples inside an error message — derives from one function, and a test fails if it drifts.

## Five things happen
to every request.

In this order, on every call. None of them is optional, and each one is recorded.

## What Vawlt does

Personal data, handled per task rather than in one sweep+
Each task declares one of two policies. Redacted — names, emails, phones, salaries and similar are replaced with typed placeholders before the model is called. As sent — the input reaches the model unchanged, because the entity data is the input; you cannot normalise a contact or summarise a deal without the names. Every response reports which happened on that call. Detection covers 14 categories, including a purpose-built salary detector that catches currency-anchored amounts, shorthand like 50k, 12 lakh or 5 crore, and bare numbers sitting near pay words. The privacy audit trail records the types of entity found and how many — never the values.
Answers checked before you get them+
Ten tasks declare a closed set of legal answers — a six-label classifier, a fourteen-action planner. After the model answers, the engine checks it and returns an error rather than passing an illegal value to your code. Nine of the ten are currently callable. Empty lists pass, because "no action needed" is a correct answer. For the CRM question-answering task there is a further guard: any person, company or email the underlying record does not support is replaced in place, leaving the rest of the answer intact.
Overload refused fast, and errors that mean something+
The in-house models are served by a single slot, so concurrent requests queue. Past a configured depth the engine returns "busy, come back in N seconds" rather than accepting the request and making you wait — with the delay computed from live queue depth against a rolling average of real service time. "You sent too much" and "we are full right now" are two distinct codes with two distinct meanings, and a saturation refusal consumes none of your allowance. One module renders every engine error for every surface, so you cannot be told "withheld" on one and "unknown task" on another.
Keys, limits and cost attribution per application+
An administrator mints a key per calling application. The raw key is returned exactly once and cannot be recovered, because only its hash is stored; keys can be listed as non-reversible fingerprints and deactivated. Rate limiting runs at 60 requests per minute per application as an abuse guard rather than a quota, shared across both request contracts, and a rejected request is not counted — so hammering does not extend the block. Cost is attributed per application, not per user or seat.
Every request logged, and a health check that tells the truth+
One row per request: the task, which model answered, tokens in and out, latency, calling application, outcome, and on a failure the error code and the upstream response body verbatim. The health endpoint checks the database, how many task adapters actually loaded against how many should have, and the queue backend. A hard dependency down returns an error; a soft problem returns success with a named warning rather than a green light. A partial adapter load is caught, because the expected count derives the same way the launcher loads them.
Quality measured on cases written to break it+
299 held-out evaluation cases across 28 tasks, deliberately written off-distribution — raw email chains, OCR noise, code-switched language, rambling four-times-length input — so they measure whether a task generalises rather than whether it matches its own templates. Three scoring tiers: deterministic structural checks, automatic grounding checks that flag invented numbers and names, and an independent model judging against the exact written rule. 87 of the 299 are a reserved holdout no promotion gate ever sees. A task with no cases reports "not evaluated" rather than a passing silence.

## A task that fails testing
gets pulled, not shipped.

An engine is only trustworthy if it can be honest about its own parts. Three mechanisms make that possible.

## Withheld, not quietly broken

A task that fails quality testing is added to a configuration list. It returns "exists but temporarily unavailable" and disappears from the catalogue, while its trained adapter stays untouched. Deliberately distinct from the error an unknown task gets. In use for two tasks today.

## Nothing promoted without a human

A retrained candidate is evaluated against held-out cases and then waits for a person to approve or reject it. Promotion is atomic, and a candidate evaluated against a baseline that has since moved is refused as stale rather than silently rolling back a newer model.

## "Approved" never means "serving" unless it is

Because adapters load at startup, an approved model is reported as staged and pending restart rather than claimed as live. The admin console holds no API key, and none may be added to it.

And what it is not, plainly. Not a chatbot — single-turn only, no conversation history, no system prompt from the caller, no streaming. Not general-purpose — a fixed catalogue, where an unknown task name is a hard error. It does not learn from use: corrections are captured and scrubbed as future training data, but the retraining step is deliberately switched off, so nothing improves on its own today. The knowledge base indexes documents but is not wired into any of the 33 tasks. Text in, text out — no video, no audio, no per-request file parsing. No confidence score is returned. 29 of the 33 tasks pass personal data through to the model, deliberately, because for those tasks the entity is the input. And there is no self-service: keys are minted by an administrator.

When they have no microphone or no connection, which is why a check runs before the round starts. For those candidates, or for anyone who assesses better in writing, the Chat Interview round is the alternative.

How accurate is the AI scoring in the voice interview?+
TalbotIQ publishes no accuracy figure. Its stated reason is that the honest measure is how often a human changed a score in your own pipeline.
